topicName: Capacity Planning, OS Tuning (Transparent Huge Pages, vm.overcommit_memory)
content: [{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Capacity Planning and OS Tuning for Redis"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Redis is an in-memory database, which means its performance and stability heavily rely on proper capacity planning and underlying operating system configurations. Inadequate memory planning or suboptimal kernel settings can lead to out-of-memory crashes, severe latency spikes during persistence, and cluster instability."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"1. Capacity Planning Fundamentals"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"When planning capacity for Redis, you must account for more than just the raw dataset size. Redis requires sufficient headroom for replication buffers, Lua scripts, client output buffers, and most importantly, the Fork operation."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Dataset Size: The actual memory consumed by your keys, values, and internal Redis metadata."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Fragmentation: Memory allocated by the memory allocator (jemalloc) that cannot be immediately reused. Monitor via mem_fragmentation_ratio."},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Copy-On-Write (COW) Headroom: When Redis performs an RDB snapshot or AOF rewrite via fork(), the OS uses Copy-On-Write. You should maintain at least 50% free RAM, or ensure maxmemory is set conservatively, to prevent the kernel from invoking the OOM killer during peak write loads."},{"order":8,"type":"subheading","text":"2. OS Tuning: Transparent Huge Pages (THP)"},{"order":9,"type":"paragraph","text":"By default, Linux uses 4KB memory pages. Transparent Huge Pages (THP) attempts to use 2MB pages to reduce Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB) misses. However, THP causes catastrophic latency and memory usage issues for Redis."},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"During a Redis fork() for persistence, if a page is modified, the entire 2MB huge page must be copied via COW instead of a single 4KB page. This drastically increases memory consumption and introduces massive CPU and latency overhead."},{"order":11,"type":"code","text":"cat /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled"},{"order":12,"type":"paragraph","text":"To check if THP is active, run the command above. It should ideally return '[never]' in brackets. To disable THP immediately at runtime, execute the following commands:"},{"order":13,"type":"code","text":"sudo echo never > /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled\nsudo echo never > /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/defrag"},{"order":14,"type":"paragraph","text":"To ensure THP remains disabled across system reboots, add the disable commands to your local startup scripts or configure a systemd service."},{"order":15,"type":"subheading","text":"3. OS Tuning: Memory Overcommit (vm.overcommit_memory)"},{"order":16,"type":"paragraph","text":"Linux kernels manage memory allocation using an overcommit policy defined by vm.overcommit_memory. The default setting (0) allows the kernel to allocate more memory than physically available based on heuristics, which is dangerous for databases."},{"order":17,"type":"bullet_point","text":"vm.overcommit_memory = 0: Heuristic overcommit (default). Can lead to OOM killer terminating Redis during fork operations."},{"order":18,"type":"bullet_point","text":"vm.overcommit_memory = 1: The kernel always overcommits. Redis explicitly recommends setting this to 1 to ensure that fork() succeeds even when system RAM is heavily utilized."},{"order":19,"type":"paragraph","text":"Configure vm.overcommit_memory to 1 immediately using sysctl:"},{"order":20,"type":"code","text":"sudo sysctl vm.overcommit_memory=1"},{"order":21,"type":"paragraph","text":"To persist this setting across reboots, append the configuration to your sysctl config file:"},{"order":22,"type":"code","text":"echo \"vm.overcommit_memory = 1\" | sudo tee -a /etc/sysctl.conf\nsudo sysctl -p"},{"order":23,"type":"subheading","text":"Summary"},{"order":24,"type":"paragraph","text":"Proper capacity planning combined with disabling Transparent Huge Pages and setting vm.overcommit_memory to 1 creates a robust foundation for running Redis in high-throughput, low-latency production environments."}]
